The final section considers national and international comparisons, such as trends among international nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and consulting practices. As an aside, Oxford may be guilty of false advertising here. According to Webster's, a handbook “is a book capable of being conveniently carried as a ready reference.” At 789 pages and 30 chapters, the book is likely to be carried around only by those engaged in some sort of weight training—an academic exercise, if you will. How to assess such a work? A chapter-by-chapter summary would be of little use, and there is no central argument to evaluate. The purpose of the book is to present the field of public management at the start of the twenty-first century. Some general themes emerge. First things first. Is it public management or public administration, and is there a difference? The answer appears to be both and no, respectively. The managerial aspects of public administration find continuity in public management, but the Handbook also makes clear that public management is concerned with the normative issues of administration (more on this point below). Public administration has become public management, and public management has become public administration. To the extent that authors consider the terms management and administration, they are treated as “synonymous” (Lynn, 28, also Frederickson, 301, and deLeon). The many contributors feel little need to explain whether they fall into an intellectual tradition of administration or management. Although the term public management is now increasingly popular, it is taken to subsume the research and questions of public administration. This is as it should be. Fashions in language should not provide a pretext to sideline earlier traditions. (And JPMRT would not roll of the tongue in the same way that JPART does.) In any case, as Frederickson notes, more recent developments in the lexicon of public sector language mean that we may be reading The Oxford Handbook of Public Governance in the future. The resolution of the administration/management question tells us something about the catholic nature of the field, whatever it is called. Tensions between frameworks or epistemologies are usually resolved via a live-and-let-live attitude. How else do we explain a Handbook that includes chapters on both economic and postmodern approaches? We are defined by what we study—public management—rather than theories or even a single epistemological approach. We cannot therefore credibly claim a distinct disciplinary perspective. At the conclusion, the editors evoke Dwight Waldo's famous description of public administration as a “subject matter in search of a discipline.” Even though they describe the field as a “theoretical car-booth sale” (726), they also conclude that the search for a discipline has been called off. The absence of a dominant and widely accepted disciplinary perspective is sometimes a weakness, preventing the type of self-confidence, coherence, and sense of progress that has allowed economics to increasingly seek to explain almost all aspects of social behavior. But the diversity of public management is also a strength, fostering a rich range of theories and perspectives, increasingly supported by well-crafted social science research. The rapid rise of JPART is perhaps the best barometer of the health of the field. You can spend an interesting day at a car-booth sale, and occasionally, you find an undervalued gem. The field has a truly international dimension, even if still dominated by Anglo-American and European perspectives. The diversity of the field makes a text such as this all the more useful. Collectively, it offers a map for the generalist to negotiate the varied terrain of public management. In particular, the section on frameworks, such as Lynn's brief history of the field, is especially useful. For the rest of the volume, I suspect that many readers will have the same experience as I, learning the most from chapters that examine areas of which I had little prior knowledge. So what are the big issues facing public management? The field maintains a clear preoccupation with the New Public Management (NPM). In their concluding comments, the editors note, “It is an exaggeration—but only a small one—to say that the Handbook has spontaneously developed an NPM center of gravity” (721). Given that the NPM is now somewhat musty, its continued importance is surprising. The NPM is no longer the new darling of the field, and many chapters, most explicitly Rubin and Kelly on budget reform, dispute that the NPM has led to any sort of convergence of practice. However, NPM clearly has had an impact in reshaping the ideas and empirical reality of public management. Regardless of the validity of the criticisms of the NPM, it has changed what we conceptualize as the study of public management: chapters related to networks, governance, public private partnerships, democratic theory, the audit explosion, culture, professionalism, performance management, functional areas, international organizations, and consulting would be far different, or perhaps not appear in this volume, without the advent of the NPM. Although some see the NPM as having an antique quality and other scholars pursue a post-NPM scholarship, it is clear that the field remains centrally if uneasily tied to ideas that became popular during the 1980s. Consistent with the rejection of the NPM convergence hypothesis, the contingent nature of claims or findings appears to be another issue on the mind of some of our most prominent scholars. The postmodern view presented by Bogason suggests that there is no scientific means to represent one reality; instead items are socially constructed, and language is a labeling device rather than a signifier of any objective truth. Although most authors fall squarely in a positivist approach that argues for the pursuit of truth, they recognize the time- and context-specific nature of that truth and are clearly concerned with challenging the idea that a rational public administration built on language conveys a common and widely understood meaning. For example, in discussing the diffusion of evaluation practices, Dahler-Larsen notes, “[t]he evaluation wave is thus both a product of and a contribution to a particular societal and cultural form. This form of explanation of the evaluation wave comes with both a functional and a symbolic emphasis” (620). Another example is Hood's proposition that public management can be understood as a faith-based movement. This is consistent with his earlier work on administrative arguments—without faith, why else should we support claims that lack clear proof. Throughout the book, we see elements of such faith-based movements behind specific ideas, for example, public-private partnerships, virtual organizations, public participation, accountability, and decentralization. These ideas carry an emotional appeal, fitting within an ideological rather than positivist view of the world. Elsewhere, Bovens explores the multiple meanings and emotional appeal of the term “accountability,” Frederickson documents the multiplicity of the term “governance,” and Pollitt examines the many dimensions of decentralization. Another basic question that recurs in the volume is how we deliver public services. Traditionally, bureaucracies have been the obvious answer, and Meier and Hill argue that bureaucracies will remain important. But there is clearly growing attention to alternative structural approaches. A well-established structural alternative is to decentralize services, a phenomenon Pollitt concisely and ably examines. But the major development here is the increased focus on networks in the delivery of public services. Not only does Frederickson devote a chapter to the concept of governance but Klijn also writes directly on networks, Skelcher considers public and private partnerships, and Smith examines NGOs and contracting. Information technology that fosters such change is also considered in chapters on virtual organizations (Margetts) and e-government (Snellen). As we become increasingly aware of the prevalence of third parties in delivering services, network theory provides a well-established theoretical framework, drawn primarily from sociology and organization behavior. Given this theoretical head start, it is easy to imagine network theory becoming the dominant analytical machinery for examining all aspects of the hollow state, subsuming less well-defined approaches such as virtual organizations, contracting, partnerships, or governance. If, as Meier and Hill claim, the study of bureaucracies will remain a pillar of public management in the twenty-first century, it is clear that networks are becoming just as important. From a research perspective, this is good news, offering an extraordinary opportunity to public management scholars. We have a useful explanatory framework that coincides with an important, growing, and understudied aspect of public management. There is a wide array of networks to study, a need to consider how “publicness” matters to networks and limited (thus far) attention to how networks operate. We need to better define the taxonomies of public networks that exist—the field should, and increasingly does, recognize there is considerable variation between network types and operations. We need to apply perennial issues in the studies of bureaucracy—structural forms, effectiveness, and accountability—to networks. Pioneering work has been done by a handful of scholars, particularly in the pages of this journal, but much more needs to be done. In particular, the study of public sector networks could benefit from the asking of what we might call normative questions. Normative questions are questions such as how should we hold public actors accountable? How should we balance democratic and administrative values? How should public actors represent the public and facilitate participation? These “should” questions have been with us since the field developed a conscious awareness of the tensions arising from placing administrative machinery in a democratic context. The editors note that “[t]he traditional public sector was defined to a considerable extent but its distinctive laws, ethics, patterns of accountability, and definition of citizenship rights” (723). Chapters such as deLeon on democracy and politics, Bertelli on administrative law, Boven on accountability, Dobel on ethics, and Ferlie and Geraghty on professions in the public sector point to the continued relevance of these normative aspects of public management. Public management scholars were late in asking such questions of the NPM, waiting until after the adoption of reforms to offer criticisms that such reforms ran contrary to legal and constitutional traditions while devaluing citizenship and public sector values. Public management scholarship usually trots behind practice, and it appears to be doing so again in the application of normative questions to networks (Klijn, 278). The reliance on third parties is based largely on a trust that such organizations will be more goal oriented, flexible, innovative, and efficient than public bureaucracies and has led to a largely implicit but popular assumption that networks should be used wherever they can be used, rather than a careful identification of the factors that make networks appropriate or not. This faith in networks evokes Hood's description of management as a religious movement and is particularly potent because networks appeal in different ways to the political ideologies of both the left and the right (Smith, 609–10). In practice, third parties often have motivations at odds with government sponsors, lack resources and management capacity, and are unstable due to uncertain funding and high turnover. However, the chapters included in the Handbook set aside faith in favor of identifying normative questions and try to answer these questions using empirical evidence. That such questions are being asked is significant, as is the limited nature of the empirical base they draw on. For example, do networks represent citizens better than bureaucracies? DeLeon suggests that networks increase the number of points of access for citizens and therefore strengthen democracy. This is equivalent to a Tocquevillian approach, says Smith, where third parties facilitate citizen participation and representation, fostering civic activity and social capital. But there is a contrary view, that third parties may be more concerned with responsiveness than equity, raise information asymmetry problems (Smith), and have opaque relationships with government (Skelcher). From this perspective, they are less consistent with democratic norms than bureaucracies. Another critical question is how we expect to hold networks accountable. The multiplicity of third parties has made it difficult even for public organizations themselves to understand who they are relying on to deliver their services (Ingraham 2005). The standard response to the accountability question appears to be a contractual approach, but as Smith points out, such an approach is often not found in practice and runs contrary to relational norms and trust that facilitate networks (also Klijn, 263). Of course, such normative questions remain important for the study of bureaucracies and indeed have bedeviled public administration throughout its history. Some might argue that the normative dimension has hobbled the field. It seems impossible to establish the core traits of a discipline when a field is dominated by questions to which there are no definitive answers. But the normative dimension is part of what puts the public in public management and must remain. Not every empirical study of a public agency or network must seek to answer a normative question. But a study of public management that does not give frequent consideration to such questions is a poor one, undervaluing the importance of the topic. One of the strengths of the Handbook is reminding us of the continuing relevance of the normative dimension of public management and to consider such issues in the context of NPM and networks. Another ongoing concern for the field is the desire to know what we are doing and whether it is effective and whether new and old service approaches to governance are delivering performance. More specifically, this includes debates about performance management and evaluations systems, as well as the effectiveness and unanticipated consequences of reform. A number of chapters deal with this directly—Talbot on performance management, Øvretveit on quality improvement efforts, Power on the explosion of audits, and Dahler-Larsen on evaluation. For a number of other authors, the issue of performance is less direct but still the driving force behind discussions of structuring incentives and information (Vining and Weimer), functional reforms (Ingraham on human resources and Rubin and Kelly on budgeting), and the use of consultants (Saint-Martin). Up to now, I have not really answered the question of whether the Handbook is any good. It is. The purpose of such a volume is not to advance new ideas but to provide an intelligent overview of the field. Here, the book succeeds admirably. Some chapters are of greater interest than others, but this is usually because of the theoretical and empirical richness of the topic being studied rather than any weakness of the authors. And, as with any overview, there will inevitably be questions about omissions—why are there no chapters on some aspects of public management that have seen empirical improvements in recent years, for example, red tape, public service motivation, or agency effectiveness? But such gripes do not take away from the achievement of the book. The Oxford Handbook of Public Management is an invaluable source for anyone interested in public management scholarship. The chapters provide an excellent starting point for researchers interested in specific areas. Many of its chapters are suitable for public management graduate courses and, in some cases, offer the most polished overview of a specific topic I have read. I have already assigned the chapter of Chun and Rainey on public and private management to my graduate students. Reading this work, it is impossible not to be struck by the diversity and vitality of the field and the continued need for better theories and strong empirical research. Perhaps the final word should be left to the editors who managed to put it all together (720): “The strange mixtures of disciplines, concerns, and instrumentaria that is the field of public management constantly moves on.”

t: Reform Gone Bad, Gone Good, and Gone Nowhere
abs: There is a revolution underway in the United States of which we all ought to take note. That revolution involves the dismantling of the civil service/merit system as we know it in a number of states, with more to follow. Several of the chapters in this volume make two core arguments, discussed below. However, other chapters do not support these two claims. This leads to two conclusions. First, the revolution is still underway and is not yet complete. In fact, it is not yet clear how many states will follow the path of the trailblazing states in terms of civil service reform. And second, the normative desirability of civil service reform is still very much open to debate. A number of chapters in Civil Service Reform in the States argue quite persuasively that civil service reform as it has been adopted and implemented in states such as Georgia and Florida is not a panacea and, in fact, may be quite detrimental to the health of the merit-based civil service as we have known it for most of the twentieth century. The two salient claims raised in several chapters of the book are these: First, a number of states are engaged in the dismantling of the traditional merit-based civil service system as we know it. And second, normatively, this is a bad thing. About half of the book's chapters focus on either the dramatic nature of civil service reform or its negative consequences. However, other chapters take a more benign view of reform or argue that it has not been as widespread as it might seem. I find both sets of arguments to be persuasive. The conclusions I draw from this book are that current efforts to revamp civil service systems in the states have been revolutionary in some states but stymied in other states and have been quite detrimental to both morale and due process in some states but more benign, even positive, in other states. The prime examples of negative reform appear to be Georgia and Florida, with Wisconsin leading the way in terms of positive reform. California appears to be a prime example where the author would like to see more rather than less reform but argues that reform has been stymied by entrenched interests, labor unions in particular. But again, from the point of view of the authors of the chapters about Georgia and Florida, California is lucky to have escaped the wrath of personnel reform. In fact, a third key claim in the book, and one consistently documented across chapters, is the importance of labor unions in understanding the extent of reform that has taken place. Civil service reform has been most dramatic where unions are weak and most successfully challenged in states where unions are strong. However, as Richard Kearney points out in his chapter, unions can play a positive role in the design and implementation of reform, and where they have, reform has been most successful. All this variation in the extent and outcomes of reform makes this book important reading for any of us who have grown up reading about the historic shifts in the United States from patronage to merit, from representativeness to responsiveness, and from concerns about equity to concerns about efficiency. The second thing that makes this book important reading is the quality of the scholars included in the volume. The volume reads like a “who's who” of the leading luminaries in the field of public administration beginning with the book's editors, Ed Kellough and Lloyd Nigro, and continuing with chapters by Hal Rainey, Sally Coleman Selden, Kathy Naff, and Norma Riccucci to name just a few. Part I of the book focuses on the nature of civil service reform and assesses both the extensiveness and desirability of reform across states. It also attempts to identify some of the factors that help us to understand the variation in the extent of reform across states. These chapters leave the reader with the impression that civil service reform in the states has been quite drastic and quite dramatic. Among the key reform efforts have been at-will hiring and broadbanding. At-will hiring removes civil service protections; instead state employees are hired and fired “at will.” Broadbanding collapses numerous, often conflicting and overlapping, pay grades into fewer, broader bands. Both these reforms provide politicians with greater flexibility. Another set of reforms aims to decentralize state personnel management by devolving personnel management from centralized personnel departments to individual agencies and managers. And a third set seeks to implement pay for performance in the states. In short, the reforms that are the focus of this book aim to give both politicians and managers greater flexibility in the hiring and firing of state employees, frequently aim to decentralize personnel decisions away from centralized personnel offices, and often use the private sector as the model for public sector reform. The chapters in Part I also raise some concerns about these reforms from a normative perspective. The chapter by Lindquist and Condrey in particular raises the issue of the impact of at-will employment on “values that we care about” such as due process and hearing rights. But other chapters in this more general and contextual part of the book also raise concerns about the enthusiasm of many in the states to jump on the reform bandwagon. What is helpful about these chapters is their identification of values—such as due process and other individual rights, social equity, responsiveness, efficiency, and effectiveness—to be used in our assessments of state-level reform. Part II of the book presents a series of case studies of reform in specific states—Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, Texas, Arizona, California, Wisconsin, and New York. This is both the most important and the weakest part of the book. It is important because of the dramatic nature of reform in states like Georgia, Florida, and South Carolina and the quite limited reforms in Arizona and California. It is weakest because of the contradictory conclusions drawn by the authors and the different metrics (or lack thereof) used. How can Kathy Naff be so disappointed about the lack of reform in California after reading about the disasters in Georgia and Florida? How do we know that Florida was a disaster? Although I find the argument presented by the Florida authors (Jim Bowman, Jonathan West, and Sally Gertz) persuasive, I would have liked some more definitive data, some sound empirical evidence. The authors of the chapters on Georgia and Texas have survey data to support their claims. But in those cases, one set of authors surveyed all state employees (supervisory and nonsupervisory, at-will and civil service), whereas the other set of authors surveyed only state agency human resources directors. Although both sets of authors acknowledge the limitations of their samples, it is difficult to draw conclusions across states when such widely divergent data are used. This is not meant as a criticism of the book reviewed here. Rather, it is a call for more research and, in particular, for the collection of better empirical data across states, on this very important subject. I highly recommend this book to anyone concerned about the quality of civil service personnel and the effectiveness of state agencies. But I also highly recommend that further research be conducted on this important subject and that further thought be given to the type of data needed to assess the success or failure of personnel reform in the states. In other words, we need to be more self-conscious about how we measure the impact and desirability of personnel reforms such as broadbanding, at-will employment, and decentralization. I began reading this book with little knowledge of the current reform movement in the states. I was shocked and amazed to learn about the lack of professionalism and centralization in some states, the experiments currently being undertaken in others, and the variation among and across states. It is a cliché to say that our federal system provides the United States with a laboratory within which to conduct experiments, but reading this book convinced me of the wisdom of that cliché in the context of personnel policy. We need to pay attention to what is happening in the states as there are many lessons to be learned about personnel management from studying them. The book reviewed here makes an important step toward identifying some of those lessons. Among those lessons are the ability of strong unions to thwart reform (New York and California), the ability to achieve reform administratively even when union and legislative support are absent (New York), the utility of using a consensus model to win support for reform (Wisconsin), the need to proceed with caution before adopting the “radical” reforms implemented in Florida, and the need to consider due process and other values before adopting wholesale personnel reform.

t: There Will Always Be a New Federalism
abs: American federalism is strongly operative and very much alive! Above all, it is opportunistic. It changes over time depending on the relative power and goals of major interests in the society. Currently, federalism has been rediscovered by liberals. This article describes the latest “New Federalism” and discusses the values of U.S. federalism at the state and grass roots' levels as well as the ways it has changed historically and has served as a force for public sector growth and the accretion of governmental functions and services.

t: Redistributive Policy and Devolution: Is State Administration a Road Block (Grant) to Equitable Access to Federal Funds?
abs: Over the last several decades, block grants have been a key instrument by which policy authority is devolved from federal to state governments. Whether the block grant approach produces more effective redistributive policy management (on equity or efficiency grounds) is an open and central question. We focus on the equity dimension by positing an explanatory framework that links access to federal block grant funding to the transaction costs associated with intergovernmental grant contracting. We argue that grant access is a function of both state-level institutional choices and the administrative capacity of local governments—which combine to influence the salient transaction costs associated with grant contracting. We apply our theoretic framework to the non-entitlement portion of the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program and analyze granting data across distinct institutional settings. We find that local administrative capacity is a key to access, indicating that some localities most in need are least equipped to capture grants, which raises equity concerns. However, the specific way in which states structure arenas of grant competition can make access more equitable. In short, we show that state-level institutional arrangements critically affect access to federal block grant funds when those funds are allocated through competitive grant contracting to local governments.

t: Connecting the Dots in Public Management: Political Environment, Organizational Goal Ambiguity, and the Public Manager's Role Ambiguity
abs: This article is a systematic effort to study a key theoretical question from the vantage point of public sector organizational behavior. Most political science models, with a primary interest in democratic control of bureaucracy, study the political influence on the bureaucracy from an agency theory perspective. Organization behavior literature, on the other hand, is focused largely on the study of individual-level phenomena in private organizations and does not incorporate political context as part of explanatory models. This article proposes a middle-range theory to “connect the dots,” beginning with disparate sources in the polity influencing organizational goal ambiguity, which in turn is expected to increase managerial role ambiguity. An empirical test, using data collected from a national survey of managers working in state human service agencies, supports this theoretical model. We find that certain types of political influence have an impact on organizational goal ambiguity, which in turn has a direct effect in increasing role ambiguity and also an indirect effect in increasing role ambiguity through organizational structure.

t: Service with a Smile
abs: James L. Perry and Ann Marie Thomson argue that civic service “lies in the uneasy tension [that exists in the American psyche] between moral individualism and civic obligation” (xv). This tension spawns a unique balancing act in the United States between classic liberalism's notion of individual liberty unfettered by government intervention and classic republicanism's bent on civic obligation to the whole of society. Defining civic service is in and of itself complicated. After outlining various definitions from the extant literature, the authors settle on an institutional perspective. This perspective defines civic service to include five key dimensions: (1) a significant commitment beyond oneself, (2) with minimal monetary reward, (3) for a defined but prolonged length of time, (4) that contributes to the benefit of the local, national, and/or global communities, (5) through formal organizational structures and programs (xvi). Perry and Thomson then employ an aggregated synthesis methodology to discern the effects of civic service on those who serve, those who receive service, and on the institutions and communities where civic service happens. This methodology moves the nascent civic service literature away from the anecdotal, single-study focus to a more systematic and empirical focus, adding significantly to the credibility of our knowledge in this arena.

t: Make or Buy?
abs: One of the highlights of my graduate school experience was reading the classic article by E. S. Savas, “The Political Properties of Crystalline H2O” (Savas 1973), which detailed the discovery by the administration of Mayor John V. Lindsay of New York City that the old public administration bromide that “there is no political way to fill a pothole” was a fallacy and there was a political price to be paid for not quickly removing snow from all the streets of the city after a major snowstorm. Since that time, Savas has been a force in public management as a scholar, practitioner, and advocate of privatization. Privatization in the City describes privatization efforts in nine large U.S. cities and attempts to assess the successes and failures that resulted. As one would expect of a book with a foreword by Rudolph Giuliani, the bulk of the book details the Giuliani administration's efforts to privatize services in New York City. The book tries to do many things: it tries to assess evidence, provide definitions and examples, and give hagiographic descriptions of bold, purposeful mayors—Giuliani and Stephen Goldsmith of Indianapolis among others—who worked tirelessly to use competition and privatization to revitalize their cities.

t: Disaster Management
abs: Publication of this collection of essays—where a number of organization theorists examine the NASA Columbia space shuttle accident in 2003—is an important event. The reason is that many of the chapter authors would be well known to readers of the leading journals of mainstream organization theory/behavior, such as Administrative Science Quarterly, the Academy of Management Journal, or Organization Science. Virtually none, by contrast, has ever published in any of the leading journals in public administration or public management. Yet here they are, examining a public organization and smack in the middle of an important public management problem. There was, of course, a time when this would not have been unusual. Much of the work that launched organization theory—by Selznick, Simon, Crozier, and, indeed, Weber—involved public organizations. But in recent decades the vast majority of scholarly writing about organizations has migrated to business schools, and almost all either is noninstitutional in locus or involves business firms. The study of public management has been left to fend for itself. This separation has not been good for mainstream organization theory, which came to pay too little attention to interesting management issues that were especially important in the public sector. It has not been good for public administration or public management scholarship, too much of which has dwelled in an intellectual ghetto. And it has not been good for government, which remains in dire need of help from scholarship for improving public performance. If this book represents, as it might, a turn toward concern with the public sector on the part of some mainstream organization scholars—a considerable number of whom do not seem particularly enchanted by studying business firms all the time, not to speak of having to deal with business school students—that is good news. The basic story told in these chapters has two parts. The first is a background to the accident created by years of low NASA funding and the effort to characterize operation of the shuttle as routine. The second is the events surrounding the accident, particularly what followed after film of the Columbia launch showed that large pieces of plastic foam had fallen off and hit parts of the spacecraft. During the 1980s and 1990s, NASA was under intense budget pressure. Dan Goldin, Bill Clinton's NASA administrator, accepted budget cuts as a contribution to the administration's priority of reducing the enormous budget deficit inherited from previous administrations rather than, as normal bureaucratic politics would have suggested, fighting the cuts. In an environment of budget cutbacks, Goldin emphasized a message of “better, faster, cheaper,” which he saw mostly as a way to challenge the agency to develop simpler technologies that might dramatically reduce space flight costs (an approach that worked spectacularly for the low-cost Mars Pathfinder), but which also ended up including reductions in the safety and program management personnel. In the George W. Bush administration, the emphasis moved to prompt and less costly execution of the International Space Station, with a specific February 2004 deadline for launch of an important space station element. This, in turn, required an increase in shuttle missions, which were necessary to supply the space station, tied to this deadline. The dislodging of foam during takeoff had been common in previous missions. The foam had earlier been considered a maintenance issue, which required repair upon the shuttle's return to earth, rather than a safety concern. However, this debris was considerably larger in size than that observed from earlier flights. It had also hit a different part of the shuttle. The significance of these differences was unknown. Boeing, a major NASA contractor, had developed a computer model that simulated the impact of debris hitting the shuttle on the structural integrity of the spacecraft, but the model only included pieces of debris much smaller than those that fell off during this launch. Interestingly, after a launch film showed debris damage, NASA appointed an ad hoc team of engineers, the Debris Action Team (DAT), to make recommendations about what actions, if any, NASA should take during the flight. To be sure, the team had less authority than a “tiger team” that would have been formed, under NASA procedures, had the foam incident been determined up front to be a significant safety problem. Nonetheless, while the flight proceeded, the team was working. And the DAT was in fact concerned about the uncertainty arising from the unusual nature of the incident compared with earlier foam debris and recommended that NASA request the air force to take images from space to see how extensive damage to the Columbia was; had such pictures been taken and showed significant damage, NASA might have attempted one of the heroic in-flight repair efforts for which it is famous. These recommendations were not ignored. They were presented to a standing-room-only internal meeting while Columbia was still in flight. However—in behavior eerily reminiscent of the shuttle program managers' dismissal of engineering criticism of the safety of O rings in cold-weather conditions in the Challenger accident in 1986—Columbia program managers rejected the recommendation of the DAT and argued there was no evidence to classify the incident as “out of family”—that is, not similar to previous debris incidents that had been classified as maintenance rather than safety issues. The argument of these chapters is that the background of budgetary pressures, deadlines, and classification of the shuttle itself as a routine operation created cognitive biases that discouraged program managers from making decisions that would have compromised the future shuttle schedule and counteracted the image that shuttle flight was a routine activity. My favorite chapters in this volume were those by Karl Weick and by Scott Snook and Jeffrey Connor. Weick's chapter on seeing NASA as an organization that needs to organize itself for high reliability, growing out of his work with Sutcliffe (2001) and Sutcliffe and Obstfeld (1999), yet again makes one stand in awe of his creative mind and graceful writing style. Weick is concerned with how an organization that faces a high degree of risk can nonetheless achieve high reliability. His short answer is that the organization needs to have a “preoccupation with failure” (164) and must constantly watch for weak signals of potential problems in its environment. Rather than relying on past interpretations and traditional categories, workers should always be on the lookout for new categories and even aim for perceptually based rather than category-based knowing. Snook and Connor's chapter, growing out of Snook's Friendly Fire (2001), one of the best books about organizations to have been published in the last decade, examines the role of the so-called diffusion of responsibility effect in the disaster. Organizations often see redundancy (backup systems) as an important way to protect against accidents. But, Snook and Connor argue, the redundancy strategy may produce a situation where nobody feels responsible for dealing with a problem, a phenomenon social psychologists studied in the l970s in trying to explain the failure of many witnesses to respond to the assault on a woman in an apartment courtyard. This same phenomenon may be modeled as a moral hazard problem, where the presence of redundancy is seen as an insurance policy. This phenomenon, Snook and Connor argue, is particularly likely to arise in the case of ambiguous signals, where it is uncertain whether a problem exists at all. Furthermore, several groups within NASA in addition to the DAT were worrying about the Columbia foam problem but did not know about each other's efforts, meaning that there was less social support for dissent from the view that the incident was not a danger. And the significant role of contractors in shuttle operations further diffused responsibility. The Snook and Connor argument is fascinating, but it is unclear that it actually explains the Columbia situation. Diffusion-of-responsibility-related unwillingness to act on a problem did not, in fact, occur in this case: the DAT did take responsibility for the problem, but program managers rejected its recommendations. The collection has a number of problems as well as its obvious strengths. One problem is that the prescription section at the end (four chapters under the heading “Beyond Explanation”) is rather weak. Also, interestingly, only one of these four chapters is authored or coauthored by an organization theorist; the others are by professors in areas such as ergonomics and aeronautical engineering. Indeed, the one chapter coauthored by an organization theorist, Starbuck himself, appears mainly to have been written by Johnny Stephenson, a NASA civil servant. This seems to reflect the fact that the culture of mainstream organization theory has often lacked any orientation toward prescription, though, to be fair, some of the other chapters include prescriptions about how NASA might improve. A second problem is that the authors seem to assume that an organization will be results- and production-oriented, and thus they are uniformly critical of NASA's “excessive” orientation to production and deadlines. This assumption would appear to reflect the authors' background of studying business firms, where such animal spirits can normally be taken for granted and their dark side explored with intellectual impunity, since any organizational course corrections that develop are unlikely to threaten firms' underlying results orientation. Such an assumption cannot, unfortunately, be made about government organizations. Many students of public management—I count myself as one—have more admiration for NASA and a greater worry that NASA might become excessively cautious and morph into “just another bureaucracy.” Likewise, many of the essays express skepticism about NASA administrator Dan Goldin's “better, faster, cheaper” campaign, which is suggested to have compromised safety to save money. Again, government organizations lack market pressures for cost savings and for organizational change, and Goldin's relentless effort to achieve both looks more attractive in a public sector context. Finally, as Starbuck and Stephenson note, there are the political problems that realistic promises can create in a government context: “When NASA has offered realistic assessments of its probable accomplishments, the media have drifted away and the public have yawned,” and budget cuts are lauded until a disaster produces the suggestion the agency had “skimped” on safety (315). A third problem is that a focus on the accident creates problems associated with selection on the dependent variable. We see analysis of a situation where there was a safety problem, efforts to attend to it were rejected, and catastrophe ensued. We do not know how common it has been for successful missions to have had safety problems that were successfully attended to. Yet surely knowledge about this is necessary to draw conclusions about NASA as an organization. We also do not know how common it has been for people to raise safety concerns that turned out not to create problems and that, had they been attended to, would have stopped shuttle launches while being examined. If such situations are common enough—and, given the argument of many of the essays that the shuttle is filled with safety risks, they may indeed be common—one does indeed need to ask the question about when risks simply must be accepted if the shuttle is ever to fly. There is an intriguing passage in one essay where a former NASA deputy administrator is quoted as saying, “I don't think there was a single launch where there was some group of subsystem engineers that didn't get up and say ‘Don't fly’” (324). I am inclined to think that one of the most interesting arguments made in this book is that NASA needs to reject the whole image of a “shuttle,” and the cognitive frame of predictable scheduling and safety associated with it. The shuttle, with its astounding numbers of quite risky subsystems and components without backups whose failure produces catastrophe, just seems to be far more dangerous than such an image suggests. The dilemma may be that, given this, making the shuttle a Weickian high-reliability organization might consume so many resources and create so many aborted flights that the shuttle would have unacceptable costs and launch delays. Woods notes, “If uncertain ‘warning’ signs always lead to sacrifices of acute goals, can the organization operate within reasonable parameters or stakeholder demands?” (297). Milliken et al. point out that in “many organizations, and particularly ones like NASA during shuttle flights, there is simply no time to debate every option and not enough resources to consider every conflicting signal” (263). Edmondson et al. argue that a Weickian approach need not consume excessive organizational resources, but “need not” does not mean “will not,” and they provide no argument that large resource requirements would not be a problem in NASA's case (241). For this reason, the single most interesting suggestion in the book—which also does not appear in the explicit prescription section—is the one by Milliken et al. that further action regarding a safety concern should be triggered where any one professional or group expresses a very strong concern there is a problem (264). One could even imagine some anonymous polling or electronic betting market analogous to the systems some companies are using to develop sales forecasts based on bets lower-level employees place. We do not want to face the possibility that the realistic alternatives for NASA might not be between an as-is shuttle program and a better version but between something like an as-is shuttle program and no shuttle at all. We are thus left still needing more essays on practical prescriptions growing out of this accident and this book's organizational analysis of it.

t: Why PART? The Institutional Politics of Presidential Budget Reform
abs: The George W. Bush administration's Program Assessment Rating Tool (PART) follows a sequence of president-initiated budget reforms. The pattern is puzzling in that past reforms have tended to drain staff resources, failed to take hold, and yielded little or no political advantage. Given the track record of past initiatives, why has the Bush administration chosen to invest Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and agency resources in PART? This article briefly traces PART's development and, placing the initiative in the context of contemporary research on the institutional presidency, attempts to make sense of the sustained appeal that rationalizing reforms have held across administrations. An account of reform as problem solving is developed. Set against the changing architecture of budget and administrative politics, reform is prompted by the interplay of evolving management concepts and two persistent problem types: Reform holds at least the potential for enhanced budget control where any leverage is valued and responds to the dilemmas of managing policy competence in the modern institutional presidency. The article concludes with a plea on behalf of institutional theories built on realistic models of how actors interpret and respond to the conditions prevailing in administrative politics.

t: Influences on the Size and Scope of Networks for Social Service Delivery
abs: Local social service agencies throughout the world have begun encouraging or requiring social service providers to form community-based networks for the delivery of publicly funded social services. Little is known, however, about the nature of the resulting networks. In this article we develop a model of organizational, programmatic, and community influences on the size and scope of interorganizational networks for social service delivery. We then apply this theoretical framework to an empirical study of service delivery networks in the Family Preservation Program in Los Angeles County. Our findings suggest that the availability of potential partners in the community, the scope of required services, and the ethnic homogeneity of the client population are key determinants of network size. We develop the implications of the results for theories of partnership formation and for more effective management of network formation processes.
